transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-01-15
Start time: 14:05 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Jonah Kim (Redwood SE), Laura Chen (FinanceCorp - Head of MLOps), Derek Hayes (FinanceCorp - CISO), Aman Singh (FinanceCorp - Infra)

Summary (auto-generated, may be rough):
FinanceCorp is evaluating Redwood for an on-prem, air-gapped deployment to serve regulated financial models. Key concerns: offline/air-gapped updates, hardware/cooling/power constraints for H100 vs A100, KMS/HSM integration for keys, audit logs and SOC2/ISO requirements, network isolation and upgrade procedures. Redwood to share security docs, schedule infra deep dive, and provide pilot pricing and hardware spec guidance.

[00:00] Maya Patel: Alright good afternoon everyone, thanks for taking the time. Uh this is Maya from Redwood, I'm the AE on the account, and with me is Jonah our SE.
[00:10] Jonah Kim: Hey folks, hi, thanks for having us.
[00:12] Laura Chen: Hi Maya, Jonah. Appreciate it. We have Derek and Aman on as well.
[00:18] Derek Hayes: Morning, or afternoon I guess. Hi.
[00:20] Aman Singh: Hey.
[00:22] Maya Patel: Nice to meet you all. The goal for today is to understand your constraints for an on-prem/air-gapped deployment and see if Redwood's Private offering can fit. We'll cover architecture, update workflow, security, and success criteria. Sound right?
[00:34] Laura Chen: Yep. High level: FinanceCorp needs to run inference for customer-facing credit risk scoring inside our network, fully air-gapped for regulatory reasons. No outgoing internet, periodic manual updates. We want to understand what the install looks like, how patches are applied, and how keys and telemetry are handled.
[00:47] Jonah Kim: Got it. So air-gapped, manual update cadence, and strict key management. Can you give a sense of hardware you currently have or are planning? GPU types, racks, power?
[00:58] Aman Singh: Right now we have a few on-prem racks with A100 80GB, but our roadmap includes H100s in Q2. However, data center power and cooling are tight so we can't just add dozens of H100s. Also we have limited physical access windows for bringing in external media.
[01:15] Derek Hayes: From security side: no outbound telemetry is allowed without approval, SAML SSO is standard, we need KMS backed by HSM, and strong auditability — logs retained per our retention policy. SOC2 and ISO27001 compliance are must-haves.
[01:29] Maya Patel: Thanks, that's clear. Jonah, do you want to walk through high-level architecture and update flows?
[01:34] Jonah Kim: Sure. So Redwood Private can be deployed as a self-managed control plane in your VPC or fully on-prem. For air-gapped setups we provide an offline bundle—it's an install artifact that you bring in via secure media. The control plane runs behind your firewall; inference runtime sits on the GPUs.
[01:49] Jonah Kim: Typical flow: initial install via air-gapped bundle, configuration of KMS endpoints (we support both internal HSMs or AWS CloudHSM if you allow dedicated network segments), and then we configure agent-based ingestion for model artifacts. Then for future updates you can apply delta bundles that we generate and you can validate checksums locally before applying.
[02:10] Laura Chen: Wait, delta bundles—how are they signed? We cannot accept unsigned binaries.
[02:14] Jonah Kim: All bundles are signed with Redwood's release key, and we provide PGP signatures and SHA256 checksums. For additional assurance, you can run the signature verification step in your staging environment. You can also request to run builds internally from our source tarball under a mutual NDA if you want full reproducibility.
[02:30] Derek Hayes: Are there options to integrate with our HSM such that keys never leave our hardware?
[02:35] Jonah Kim: Yes, we support local HSM integration—your KMS can store model encryption keys and TLS certs. The runtime can call out to the HSM via PKCS#11 or KMIP depending on your setup.
[02:46] Aman Singh: About telemetry: you said offline—does Redwood rely on telemetry for model performance or crash reporting? We can't allow auto-sends.
[02:53] Maya Patel: We understand. For air-gapped deployments telemetry is disabled by default. You can enable local logging to files, and we can provide an ops bundle that you can pull manually to share support logs. Any outbound diagnostics require explicit opt-in.
[03:07] Derek Hayes: Good. On network isolation: we use strict VLAN segmentation and no NAT to the internet from the inference racks. How does license activation or DRM work in that case?
[03:18] Jonah Kim: License activation can be done via an offline license token. We can generate a token based on your deployment fingerprint. The token file is applied during install. For renewals we can do rolling license tokens with expiration and offline renewal procedures.
[03:30] Laura Chen: Okay, that helps. Another question: we run a bunch of microservices that call the model via an internal LB. Is Redwood runtime compatible with our sidecar mesh — we use Istio?
[03:40] Jonah Kim: Yes, the runtime exposes standard HTTP/gRPC endpoints. Folks usually put it behind an internal load balancer, and for mTLS Istio sidecar works fine. We do recommend CPU pinning for the runtime control plane processes to avoid noisy neighbor issues.
[03:52] Aman Singh: Hardware constraints: if we can't fit many H100s, can we run a mixed cluster of A100 and H100? How does Redwood handle scheduling?
[04:01] Jonah Kim: We support mixed clusters. The scheduler is model-aware: it can route model variants to GPUs that meet the memory/compute profile. You can also set routing policies—prefer low-latency GPUs or prefer cost-effective ones. In an on-prem setup you can pin model versions to specific worker groups.
[04:17] Laura Chen: About model updates—if we have internal models that get retrained weekly, how do we push them into the runtime if it's air-gapped?
[04:25] Jonah Kim: For customer models you would package a model artifact and transfer via secure media to the inference cluster. We provide a CLI tool that validates and imports the model local to the cluster. The import process can be automated with a scheduled offline job if you have an internal transfer cadence.
[04:40] Derek Hayes: We want to ensure reproducible builds and hash verification. Will Redwood provide signed model manifests and the tool to validate them?
[04:48] Jonah Kim: Yes, model manifests include checksums and a signature. The CLI verifies signatures and manifests before loading into the runtime.
[04:55] Maya Patel: From commercial POV—we typically have a dedicated deployment and an enterprise license for Private, plus a monthly support tier. For pilots we can do a time-limited license and a support bundle.
[05:07] Laura Chen: What's the fallback story if a node fails? Do we get graceful degradation?
[05:12] Jonah Kim: The runtime supports graceful degradation—requests can be retried to other replicas. For air-gapped clusters you might want a small replication factor per model; we can help you size that based on expected qps and SLOs.
[05:23] Aman Singh: Power and cooling: if we put H100s in, we need to account for 600–700W per card in worst case. Our telemetry suggests rack PDU limits. Do you provide a hardware spec doc?
[05:35] Jonah Kim: Yes, we'll share a hardware spec that includes per-card power draw, recommended airflow, and suggested chassis. Also guidance for NVLink topologies and PCIe lane requirements.
[05:46] Derek Hayes: Compliance: we'll need SOC2 coverage and vendor evidence. Can you send SOC2 report and ISO certs?
[05:52] Maya Patel: Absolutely. We'll send our SOC2 Type II and ISO27001 certs. For on-prem customers we also include architecture and security design docs.
[06:00] Laura Chen: How about software patching windows? We can't have nightly reboots.
[06:06] Jonah Kim: Patches are scheduled per your maintenance windows. For critical security fixes you can opt-in for an emergency patch workflow; for everything else patches are bundled and applied during agreed maintenance windows. We also provide an ability to stage and test patches in a non-production clone before rolling.
[06:21] Derek Hayes: You mentioned the option to build from source—how realistic is that? We may want to vet code.
[06:26] Jonah Kim: Under NDA we can provide source bundles and build instructions. Some customers request to run their own builds. It's a more involved process but we support it for high-compliance customers.
[06:36] Maya Patel: Quick question: any initial blockers, from your side, that would prevent moving forward with a pilot?
[06:42] Laura Chen: The main blocker is a clear offline update process and a pilot pricing that accounts for our limited rack space. Also legal needs to review data processing addendum.
[06:51] Derek Hayes: Also we need KMS/HSM integration docs and assurance that keys never leave our HSM.
[06:57] Maya Patel: Understood. We'll prioritize the security pack and the HSM integration guide.
[07:02] Jonah Kim: For the pilot we often deliver a 4-node cluster (mixed A100/H100) as a starting point with documented sizing. We'll propose options that work within your power and cooling constraints.
[07:13] Aman Singh: If we go forward, who owns OS updates? We prefer to manage base OS and you manage runtime.
[07:19] Jonah Kim: That's a common split: customer manages host OS and infra, Redwood manages runtime and model lifecycle. But we can adjust to your operations model.
[07:28] Laura Chen: Any concerns about model quality drift monitoring without internet?
[07:33] Maya Patel: You can run local evals and Redwood Optimize can be configured to run locally with evaluation bundles. We can provide tooling for offline quality checks and integration into your internal CI.
[07:45] Derek Hayes: About licensing: do you support per-instance licensing or core-based?
[07:50] Maya Patel: We have a few models—per-node, per-GPU, or committed capacity. For Private, customers often choose a per-GPU committed model with a support tier. We'll include pricing options in the follow-up.
[07:59] Laura Chen: Can you share a sample SLA for Private deployments?
[08:03] Maya Patel: Yes, sample SLA and support level descriptions will be included in the pack.
[08:08] Jonah Kim: Also, on backups and disaster recovery: we recommend regular encrypted model backups to internal offline storage. For air-gapped clusters you can have a procedure to rotate backup media and store off-site per policy.
[08:21] Aman Singh: One more infra detail: do you have specific kernel modules or drivers we need on the host that may conflict with our existing stack?
[08:29] Jonah Kim: We rely on standard NVIDIA drivers and Docker/container runtimes. We'll provide exact driver versions and kernel module requirements. In many cases customers run the runtime in OCI containers compatible with their orchestration.
[08:42] Laura Chen: Thanks, this is helpful. Next steps recap?
[08:46] Maya Patel: Recap: Redwood to send security pack (SOC2/ISO, HSM/KMS integration, offline bundle verification steps, hardware spec) by Friday 2025-01-17. Jonah to schedule infra deep dive for week of 2025-01-20. Redwood to share pilot pricing and agreement by 2025-01-18. FinanceCorp to share compliance checklist by 2025-01-22.
[09:05] Derek Hayes: Sounds good.
[09:07] Laura Chen: We'll review and get back with preferred times for the deep dive.
[09:10] Aman Singh: I'll gather power/cooling reports and share with Jonah.
[09:13] Maya Patel: Great — thanks everyone. We'll follow up with calendar invites and the docs.
[09:17] Jonah Kim: Thanks all, talk soon.

End of transcript.

Notes on transcription quality: audio was clear; some brand names may have been transcribed imperfectly (e.g., HSM vendor names). There were a few cross-talk moments and filler words left in for authenticity.
